messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Hey folks, we have an L3 flyer on the team. Design a rocket that goes about 8,000 m. What would you build?

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: One altitude, about 8,000 m, so the band is 7,600 to 8,400 m. Nothing is said about landing speed, wind, rail, or site, so the usual gates apply: touchdown at or under 6 m/s, 2 m/s wind, 1.5 m rail, sea level. "L3 flyer" means the team can fly an M, N, or O, not that the motor class is pinned. Drag-free speed for 8,000 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 8000) = 396 m/s, so this is a big motor, not a cluster of Gs.
2. Feasibility: An L or M on a slim tube has been landing nearer 4 km in this catalog's impulse range, so I want something in the O class, or an O with a small upper stage if one motor falls short. Impulse has to stay at or under 40,960 N*s. I will look up an O, an M, and an N before drawing anything.

2. Feasibility: Cesaroni 21062O3400-P is class O, 21041 N*s, 3421 N average, 6.14 s, 98 mm by 1.239 m, 16.842 kg with 11.272 kg of propellant, and only a 0 s delay. The N5800 is the same case size and almost the same impulse, 20367.7 N*s, but it burns in 3.53 s, so it spends more of the flight at high speed. The M1297W is only 5413.8 N*s. I will fly the O alone. 21041 N*s is under the 40,960 N*s cap. On a guessed 22 kg rocket, liftoff thrust-to-weight is 3421 / (22 * 9.81) = 15.8. Half the mass is propellant, so the fins have to be large or the margin dies mid-burn.
3. Size: At 5.5 m/s the canopy area is 2 * 22 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5.5^2) = 14.6 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 14.6 / 3.1416) = 4.3 m. I will use 4.6 m so the landing stays under 6 m/s once the airframe comes in heavier than the guess. Tube outer diameter 0.110 m, mount 0.102 m, which clears the 0.098 m case.
4. Draft: Fiberglass ogive 0.45 m on a 1.85 m fiberglass tube, wall 3 mm. O3400 plugged, electronic 4.6 m chute at apogee. Mount 0.102 m by 1.28 m. Three fiberglass fins, root 0.38 m, tip 0.15 m, span 0.28 m, sweep 0.18 m, 6 mm thick. Sea-level defaults.

4. Check: The simulator gives 7490.8 m, about 6% under 8,000 m, so it misses the 7,600 m floor of "about 8,000". Everything else is legal: rail exit 23.0 m/s, thrust-to-weight 13.9, margin 2.66 cal at the rail and 2.66 cal through the burn, landing 4.4 m/s with the chute out at 32.6 s. Mass is 25.2 kg. The branch is still in the air at 1199.8 s, which is the clock, not a fast landing. The fins are bigger than this margin needs.
5. Fix: 7490.8 m is the miss. I am cutting fin span from 0.28 m to 0.20 m and root from 0.38 m to 0.30 m, tip 0.12 m, sweep 0.14 m. That drops drag while 2.66 cal of margin has room to give. Motor, tube, and the 4.6 m chute stay.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: The simulator gives 8159.6 m, inside the 7,600 to 8,400 m band around 8,000 m. Rail exit 23.5 m/s, thrust-to-weight 14.2, margin 2.61 cal at the rail and 2.58 cal through the burn, landing 4.4 m/s with the chute out at 34.0 s. Mass 24.6 kg. The branch is still up at 1199.8 s, same clock as before, and 4.4 m/s is under 6 m/s.
5. Fix: 8159.6 m is in band and the gates pass, so I am leaving the fins where they are.
6. Uncertainty: Mach 2.18 makes the drag warning real, so 8159.6 m could move a few hundred metres either way. The 4.4 m/s figure is the descent rate when the run hits 1199.8 s, not a recorded touchdown, because a soft fall from this height does not finish inside the clock. Cd 0.8 on a 4.6 m canopy is optimistic, and 2 m/s of wind over that long a hang time is why the drift is near 1,900 m.
